title: Problem 07
markdown:
### Problem
Show that there are infinitely many pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers such that $a^2 + b^2 = n^{2015}$ for some integer $n$.

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
Let $p$ and $q$ be any positive integers, and define $n = p^2 + q^2$.

Choose:

$$a = (p^2 + q^2)^{1007} p \quad \text{and} \quad b = (p^2 + q^2)^{1007} q.$$

Then $a$ and $b$ are positive integers, and:

$$\begin{aligned} a^2 + b^2 &= \left[(p^2 + q^2)^{1007} p\right]^2 + \left[(p^2 + q^2)^{1007} q\right]^2 \\ &= (p^2 + q^2)^{2014} p^2 + (p^2 + q^2)^{2014} q^2 \\ &= (p^2 + q^2)^{2014} (p^2 + q^2) \\ &= (p^2 + q^2)^{2015} = n^{2015}. \end{aligned}$$

Since there are infinitely many pairs of positive integers $(p, q)$, this construction produces infinitely many distinct pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers.

### Conceptual Explanation
Setting $n = p^2 + q^2$, multiplying by the power $(n^{1007})^2 = n^{2014}$ scales the sum of squares $p^2 + q^2 = n$ up to $a^2 + b^2 = n^{2015}$. Any choice of $(p, q)$ generates a valid pair.

### Key Technique
Power scaling construction $(n^k p)^2 + (n^k q)^2 = n^{2k+1}$.
